Question: I’m 40 and an occasional cannabis smoker (joints and vapes). I’d go 2 weeks in a row of 2-2 hit night in a row every other month or so. This trend started up again after about 10 years of not touching weed. Would this be enough to cause emphysema?

If you drive a gas-powered car or live in an area polluted by drivers or such, if you’re around people who intentionally smoke just about anything, and probably if you blow out your birthday candles each year and inhale traces of smoke from those blown-out candles… or all of those combined could, in some sense of meaning, be said to have contributed as a “cause” for a person getting emphysema. For the most part only the more extreme exposures (Living in the heart of Tokyo, tending nightly campfires or commercial fry-kitchens, direct “first-hand” of tobacco or marijuana, and other such things are the sort of thing to worry about in this regard. There is also a very small portion of the population (about 1 person in a thousand or less with a genetic defect known as AAT-1 (Alpha Antitrypsin Deficiency) that will tend to get COPD as they get older in life regardless of any exposures, and will get it somewhat younger with such exposures. The amount of smoking you describe would likely have no or almost no measurable effect in pretty much all the non-AAT-1 population (i.e. better than 99% of the population) although with any such medical statistical things it might still get listed as a “contributing factor” or somesuch. NOTE: I am NOT a doctor, nor do I have medical training of any kind, although I’ve read and written extensively about the effects of smoking and exposure to other folks’ smoke. So bear that in mind when evaluating what I’ve written.

That discomfort limited me to just a few pubs in my area and COVID limited that even more… so I ended up basically kicking my pub habit and simply staying at home for a good part of the last few years. Mats, where we differ is my staunch belief that “addiction” is largely individualized rather than rule of thumb chemical, when it comes to most people. Your advice may be quite sound for some, maybe even many, people out there. But for some others, maybe even many others, I believe it greatly overstates the amount of dependence that we classically associate with true addiction.

Question: I’ve been vaping for 3 years. I use my vape about 10-15 times a day. How much has this affected my health?

So even if vaping was just like smoking (and it’s certainly NOT — e.g. there’s no carbon monoxide and virtually no carcinogens etc compared to cigarettes) — but even if it was just like smoking you vaped about half the daily amount for about 1/5th of time as the women smokers. Half of a fifth is a tenth. The study cited above noted those smokers, smoking ten times the amount that you vaped still only had 3% of the risk of lifelong smokers. If the change in risk is linear (Antismokers will claim it’s not… but they’ll claim almost anything if it’s in their favor: they’re no better than Big Tobacco in that regard.) … if it’s linear then you’d be affected, on average, less than 1/2 of 1% of the risk experienced by all those older smokers you see out there. And in reality, since the vapor is WAYYYY less “deadly” than the smoke, your risk would be even far less than that… probably more like 1/10th of one percent of the risk of a lifelong smoker. So I don’t think you have too much to worry about, BUT… I should make VERY clear: I am not a doctor, nor have any medical training, although I have written two books regarding the subject.

Question: Can smoked cigarettes make you lose weight or not?

HOWEVER… the health benefit is at least pretty questionable since those increases also tend to “wear out” one’s organs when they are constant and repeated. I am NOT a doctor, but I think most doctors would agree that being 10 or 20 pounds overweight is likely significantly healthier in the long run than smoking. Every individual is different though. For many smokers, smoking acts a little “reward”, something that makes you feel good and that you interpret as not all that different than the enjoyment one might get from eating some chocolate. Some smokers find that they make a trade in: if they stop smoking they start eating more chocolate and they end up healthier in some ways… but unhealthier in other ways if that increase moves into the 25, 50, or 100 pound range. So, emphasizing once again that I’m not a doctor, I would say cigarettes can have a positive weight-loss (or at least avoidance of weight gain) result, particularly if we’re looking at a “post-quitting” effect, but that for most people, overall, they’re likely to be healthier in the long run if they’re one of the runs who only puts on ten or twenty pounds while ditching a pack a day habit.

Question: How dangerous is secondhand smoke if I am exposed to it everyday in summer when opening the windows?
Answer: I started this as a response to a comment, but then realized the commenter has not been posting for the last four years so it wouldn’t really be fair to hit them with an extensive criticism they’d likely never see for a response. However, my response actually serves quite nicely as an answer in and of itself! :) Here ye be: (A responder wrote) “Secondhand smoke is as harmful as if you smoked, yourself, and inhaled.” Not really. That gives the impression to the asker that it’s almost like they smoked a cigarette themselves in the few seconds of opening a window or were exposed to wisps of smoke that might happen to blow in over short occasional time spans while breezes and winds would be blowing it all over the place from a fair distance outside (If smokers regularly hung out a few feet from the window the asker would most definitely have noted that in their question!) Think about the reality of the amount they’d inhale. If they were in a moderate sized room with modern decent levels of ventilation for the full ten minutes of a person smoking a cigarette in that room, they would actually be inhaling only about a thousandth (maybe even only a ten-thousandth if the room was a bit large and the ventilation was good) of the volume of air that the secondary smoke would be dispersed through. Do the math yourself on breathing volume at rest and the room size and air changes… I think you’ll find I’m right. Additionally, in terms of the question, any smoke making its way to and through the various windows being opened would be FAR less than one would get sitting in a room with a person smoking. How much less? Depends on distance and wind patterns, but likely at least 100 times less. The main “danger” that’s supposedly been shown from secondary smoke was summed up in the EPA Report in the 1990s that resulted in smoking bans flying in everywhere. But what that study actually found was a *barely* sort-of statistically significant relationship that would cause one extra case of lung cancer out of every thousand workers exposed for EIGHTY THOUSAND WORK HOURS of smoke through their working lifetime. So the asker would really likely be up to close to 1 extra chance in a billion of lung cancer even if they spent years opening such windows on temperate days. And that “one-in-a-billion” type finding actually FAILED normal statistical significance standards of 95% and the EPA claimed significance anyway! (Heh, they kind of HAD to: I believe they’d put out a statement or press release a year BEFORE the study that indicated that that was what their study would find! LOL!)

Question: Can you preheat water in a shower?
Answer: I am not a plumber, but I believe that to some degree you can Or At least that you should be able to.) The tanks are designed to come on and heat the water when a thermostat senses that it has dropped below a certain temperature, say"X", and heat the tank's water back up to the top of the range you've picked as desirable, say X+15, and then shut off until the temp drops below its range again. In the course of an ordinary longish shower, if it had been mid-range at the start, it might take two minutes or so for the tank heater to come on and then it would be trying to compete with heating fresh cold water while you are simultaneously pulling out hot water. IF however, while you are in the initial stages of getting your fresh clothes etc, you had turned the hot water on at full blast for sixty or ninety seconds, you’d have triggered you heater to come on. Then you turn the water off, and spend five or so minutes getting set, and THEN adjust the faucets to your temperature and start your shower. You’ll be starting while the tanks water has been preheated to its maximum heat and the result should be a longer period of water as hot as you like. If you **REALLY** want to max this idea out, have a confederate watch and time the heater in the basement and call you on your smartphone when the heater comes on and again when it’s gone off. Do that on three occasions to get a true average and you’ll be able to use that average timing for future preheats! Heh, your confederate can also check the water heater thermostat and perhaps turn it up. HOWEVER… IF YOU SHARE THE SAME SYSTEM AS OTHERS… you need to let them know what you’re planning and get their agreement. Otherwise they might turn their shower on as usual, then hop in and find themselves with scalding water pouring on them! So yeah, SERIOUSLY, *do* check with others before making any changes!
